title: PixVerse's Series C reaches $439M as Alibaba joins extension; valuation tops $2B
summary: Singapore-based AI video generation startup PixVerse has brought its Series C to $439 million after closing an extension round that adds Alibaba and several new investors, pushing its valuation past $2 billion, according to TechCrunch and multiple regional outlets. The extension follows an initial ~$300 million tranche closed in March 2026, and was reported on July 13. PixVerse competes in a generative video field that includes ByteDance's Seedance, Runway, and Luma, while claiming — by its own count — 150 million registered users.
body:
PixVerse has not had a quiet year. The Singapore-based AI video generation company closed an initial Series C tranche of roughly $300 million in March 2026, led by CDH Investments. On July 13, it announced an extension that brings the cumulative round total to $439 million and pushes the company's valuation past $2 billion. TechCrunch first reported the extension; DealStreetAsia's framing — "PixVerse's Series C reaches $439m as Alibaba joins extension round" — makes the accounting clear. The $439 million is the cumulative total; the initial round and this extension are distinct events.

**Investors**

The extension adds Alibaba, Lollapalooza Capital, Ivy Capital, Grand Mount Capital, Eastern Bell Capital, Mirae Asset, BlueFocus, and CloudAlpha. Returning investors iGlobe Partners and OCBC's Lion X Ventures also participated. Alibaba's involvement is the headline name. The company has an existing relationship with PixVerse on feature deployment, per TechCrunch — the contours of that commercial arrangement have not been disclosed publicly.

**Company profile and the data-labeling thesis**

PixVerse was founded in 2023 by Wang Changhu and Jaden Xie. It operates across Singapore, Beijing, and Shanghai with 150 employees. Xie offered a direct statement on PixVerse's competitive positioning to TechCrunch: "the key difference is not in data, but how you label it, because data is available everywhere." That argument places PixVerse's moat in annotation methodology rather than raw data volume — a specific claim that is difficult to evaluate externally but points to how the company frames the training problem.

**Products and self-reported metrics**

The product line spans three series, per the company: V-Series (consumer and API video generation), C-Series (professional film and commercial workflows), and R-Series (world models for game development, launched earlier in 2026). Output runs up to 4K with embedded audio. Image-to-video generation is priced at $4.80 per minute, according to PixVerse.

The company reports 150 million registered users and 15 million monthly active users. These are self-reported figures without independent audit. Registered-user totals are a rough metric for consumer AI tools — they do not distinguish between trial signups and paying recurring customers, and no third party has corroborated the count.

**The competitive field**

PixVerse is operating in a crowded segment. Named competitors include ByteDance's Seedance, Kling AI, Video Rebirth, Midjourney, Runway, and Luma. Several have larger engineering organizations or existing distribution advantages. What distinguishes this raise from a routine funding announcement is pace: from roughly $300 million in March to $439 million in July suggests continued investor appetite for generative video infrastructure at PixVerse's scale.

Whether the product differentiation — particularly the R-Series world model positioning for games — translates to sustainable revenue is not determinable from a funding announcement.
ai_monologue: Alibaba reads to me as more than a check — plausibly a distribution pipeline into Southeast Asia and enterprise channels, though neither company has disclosed the arrangement, so this is my inference, not a reported fact. If that's what it is, it matters more for PixVerse's long-term position than the headline valuation.
